_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Cariboo Voices & Local News' — stories FROM and ABOUT the Cariboo-Chilcotin region and its communities. Score 80-100 for articles directly covering: news and events in Williams Lake, Quesnel, 100 Mile House, Bella Coola, Horsefly, Likely, Anahim Lake, Alexis Creek, or the Cariboo Regional District; local government and civic decisions (City of Williams Lake, City of Quesnel, CRD, District of 100 Mile House); local health services and emergency closures; local economy, businesses, and community programs; Cariboo arts, culture, and community events; AND digital equity, rural internet access (fiber, fixed wireless, Starlink), and connectivity serving these specific communities. Articles from local Cariboo news sources (mycariboonow.com, wltribune.com, quesnelobserver.com, 100milefreepress.net, cfjctoday.com) covering Cariboo community life should score 65-85. Score 50-79 for: BC provincial news directly affecting Cariboo communities, rural Canadian community stories closely paralleling Cariboo life, digital equity and rural internet broadly. Score 20-49 for: general BC news that may affect rural areas, broader rural Canada topics without specific Cariboo tie-in. Score 0-19 for: national/international news without Cariboo relevance, pure tech or entertainment with no community angle. Penalise heavily (score 0–20): international geopolitical and war news with no Cariboo tie-in; science discoveries without a local community connection; consumer tech reviews and gadget guides; wildlife and conservation stories not involving Cariboo communities or First Nations; BC provincial news without direct Cariboo-region relevance. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Each extra hour of prolonged sitting linked to 9% higher cancer death risk
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Sitting for long, uninterrupted stretches may carry greater health risks than sitting the same amount of time in shorter bouts. Researchers found that each extra hour of prolonged sedentary behavior was associated with a 9% higher risk of cancer death. Breaking up sitting with movement showed the opposite pattern, while replacing an hour of prolonged sitting with light activity was linked to a 12% lower risk.

items.title: [Kagi Small Web] The Disappearing Bottom Rung in L&D
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Philippa Hardman, Dr Phil's Newsletter, Sept 03, 2026

This is an interesting take. Philippa Hardman explains the 'disappearance' of entry-level roles in learning and development as a consequence of the way AI is replacing human work at those lower levels. Nothing new there. But then comes the observation, "L&D work is going from a craft you learned by doing - producing courses, mastering tools, making things - to a discipline you're trusted to exercise: diagnosing problems, specifying solutions, judging quality and measuring impact." I wonder whether this is true - the professions I can think of, such as engineering, medicine and law, all depend a lot on developing through experience the sort of intuition and socialization needed to be 'professional'. Learning, in other words, by doing.

items.title: [ArchDaily] From Residual Land to Civic Places: 6 Mexican Public Parks
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Mexico's rapid urban growth over recent decades has left many cities struggling with fragmented neighborhoods, high crime rates, and severe shortages of quality public spaces. In many low-income urban areas, informal development occurred alongside raw infrastructure like drainage canals, rail lines, and steep ravines, dividing communities and creating hazardous vacant zones. To address this spatial segregation and lack of civic amenities, public agencies and architects across Mexico are intervening in these abandoned buffer zones to construct public parks. By converting former physical barriers into accessible pedestrian corridors, these projects rejoin separated neighborhoods, re-establish safe visual sight lines, and provide spaces for community gathering and daily recreation.

items.title: [Krebs on Security] Two Alleged ‘TeamPCP’ Hackers Arrested in Australia
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Authorities in Australia have arrested two men believed to be members of TeamPCP, a prolific cybercrime and data extortion group blamed for perpetrating the longest running spree of software supply chain attacks ever. In a statement released today, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) said two unnamed suspects from Western Australia, aged 21 and 23, were arrested in connection with a "sophisticated cybercrime syndicate that allegedly created malicious open-source software to rob thousands of global businesses." The AFP did not name the defendants, but KrebsOnSecurity learned the 21-year-old suspect's real identity in June, and has been communicating with him ever since. This story includes interviews with TeamPCP's self-described spokesperson, and examines clues left behind by the TeamPCP leader that likely led to his undoing.

items.title: [Fast Company] What is public interest technology and how does it help people in need? A policy expert explains
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Every year, millions of people who qualify for food assistance never get it. The money exists and they meet the eligibility rules, but they don’t know that the program exists, or if they qualify. For others, the application is too long and complicated.

Public interest technology can fill these gaps between what a policy promises and what a person experiences.

Public interest technology is a combination of technology, data, design, policy, social science, ethics and law brought together to improve people’s lives and serve the common good. Public interest technology has prevented children from being poisoned by lead paint, helped families stay in their homes instead of being evicted, and supported disaster recovery efforts after the Los Angeles fires.

The work is carried out by government agencies, nonprofit organizations, universities, community groups and experts like me who study how to use technology to help solve societal issues.

How a solution arises

Public interest technology starts with identifying the problem and asking two questions: What system is not working for the people it is supposed to serve? And how can it be improved?

The next step involves building a cross-disciplinary team to address the situation and scoping the problem. A caseworker, for example, knows things that no analyst can discover from data. A community member knows the reality on the ground. Data scientists, designers, engineers and policy experts, as well as the people affected, create the technology together.

Once there is an initial design for a solution, the team iteratively develops the system, validates that it functions as intended, evaluates whether its impact is equitable, and field-tests it to reveal errors and measure impact.

Impact is the bottom line. A pilot program that ends in an academic paper or a press release does not help people. Impact means the system works, the community trusts it and uses it, and people’s lives improve.

Who the technology helps

Chicago used to wait until a child’s blood test came back positive for lead before inspecting a home for lead sources. That sequence protects the next child who will live there, but not the current one. A data-driven system that we helped develop tracks housing stock, building permits and health information in order to flag high-risk housing units, allowing the health department to conduct preventive inspections before a child gets poisoned.

Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, has a limited budget to help the 10,000 to 15,000 people who receive eviction notices each year. A machine learning system now identifies the residents most likely to become homeless, so the county’s limited outreach efforts and scarce dollars reach the people who need help the most.

Johnson County, Kansas, linked its jail system, emergency medical service and mental health service so it could identify people cycling between crisis and incarceration. The system helps mental health workers identify and reach out to people at risk before the next arrest.

Some cities are expanding public interest technology in-house. New York just launched the Public Interest Technology Crew, which embeds technology specialists in agencies to solve problems for residents. The first crew, embedded in the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, is building a portal for New Yorkers to report violations of click-to-cancel subscription laws.

Organizations such as the U.S. Digital Corps, Coding it Forward and Data Science for Social Good (which I co-founded) are creating partnerships between technology specialists and employees in governments and nonprofits. And universities are starting to weave public interest technology into curricula, largely driven by the Public Interest Technology University Network, a consortium of universities, cities and foundations.

What makes a technology a public interest technology is a set of choices: who helps build it, how its success is defined, and who is accountable when it gets things wrong. Made correctly, those choices mean the person who qualifies for food assistance isn’t left waiting for it.

Rayid Ghani is a distinguished career professor of machine learning and public policy at Carnegie Mellon University.

items.title: [Fast Company] Google is helping bring cutting-edge battery tech to an old West Virginia strip mine
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

For decades, a sprawling site in West Virginia was mined for coal, and part of the operation is still active. But on a 500-acre section abandoned 20 years ago, something new is taking shape: a clean-energy project pairing solar power with cutting-edge battery technology that could help renewables deliver electricity around the clock.

The $350 million project, called Mammoth Solar, will sell energy to Google, which has a goal to get to 24/7 carbon-free energy on every grid where it operates. It’s the first development where the tech giant will rely on zinc batteries, an emerging long-duration technology that can store electricity for 10 hours.

It’s the next step in the evolution of renewable energy. A decade ago, most solar and wind projects didn’t include batteries at all, says Jon Yoder, president and CEO of MN8 Energy, which partnered with Google to build and operate the new plant. “There was no economically viable way to store that power when the sun wasn’t shining or the wind wasn’t blowing,” he says.

A few years later, lithium-ion batteries became viable for short-term storage. They work well for storing electricity for about four hours, helping cover the evening spike in demand after the sun goes down. But using them to bridge longer gaps remains too expensive.

MN8 and Google researched new options for long-term storage that could be used along with lithium-ion batteries, and “ran literally dozens of different combinations of technologies to compare the functionality against the cost,” Yoder says.

Zinc stood out, he says, because the batteries have a relatively high round-trip efficiency, meaning the amount of electricity you get out for the amount that you put in. The zinc batteries, made by a company called Eos, also use sustainable materials and don’t pose a fire risk.

“We chose to support Eos’s batteries because the chemistry relies on Earth-abundant materials—zinc and bromine—and a more resilient supply chain than traditional lithium-based systems,” says Campbell Howe, advanced energy program manager at Google. 

“Additionally,” Howe says, “Eos’s manufacturing facility in Pennsylvania is already stood up, which will continue to support job growth and economic development in the Appalachian region.”

The project will break ground in 2027, with 86 megawatts of solar panels in place by 2028; 70 megawatts of lithium-ion storage will be added by 2029, followed by 10 megawatts of the zinc batteries in 2030.

The zinc technology is still a relatively small amount of the project. “Because this is relatively new technology and because we want to see how it performs in real-world situations over an extended period of time, we sized it in a way where the economic investment still is prudent even with the remaining risks that could be latent in the business model for the zinc,” Yoder says.

But it’s a meaningful amount, and it will let both MN8 and Google see how the zinc batteries perform, including their real-world efficiency, to help plan future projects.

As the lithium-ion batteries cover the evening, the new batteries can help cover more of the night. “We can serve those hours from, let’s say, 10 at night until 8 the next morning, when the sun is coming up again,” Yoder says.

Because the zinc batteries are a smaller piece of the development, the project isn’t yet designed to provide energy all the time, “but that’s the theory of where we’re headed,” he says. “These three technologies, in combination between solar, short duration, and long duration, move the needle much closer to the ability to serve power on a 24/7 basis.”
